---
title: "How a game is played"
guide-section: "Understanding replaylab"
---

This page follows one game from the first round to the score: who calls whom, where
the clock moves, and how a bought design's result travels from the lab back to the
player. Most of it is the life of one batch. The last section says exactly what keeps
the results of designs not bought out of a player's reach, and what does not.

# The objects

| object | where | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`Episode`](../reference/engine.episode.Episode.qmd) | `engine/episode.py` | one game and one player; `play()` is the game loop |
| [`Player`](../reference/engine.episode.Player.qmd) | `engine/episode.py` | anything with `play_round(campaign)` and `finish(campaign)` |
| [`ScriptedPlayer`](../reference/engine.episode.ScriptedPlayer.qmd) | `engine/episode.py` | asks a scripted policy for each batch |
| [`LLMPlayer`](../reference/eval.llm_player.LLMPlayer.qmd) | `eval/llm_player.py` | runs model turns; the model acts through tools |
| [`ReplayEnvironment`](../reference/engine.replay.ReplayEnvironment.qmd) | `engine/replay.py` | the game: campaign, store, hidden scoring context |
| [`Campaign`](../reference/engine.Campaign.qmd) | `engine/campaign.py` | the rules; the only object that talks to the lab |
| [`CampaignStore`](../reference/store.CampaignStore.qmd) | `store/` | SQLite: batches, delivered results, the clock, events |
| [`ReplayBackend`](../reference/backends.ReplayBackend.qmd) | `backends/replay.py` | the stand-in for the lab; holds every result |
| [`CampaignState`](../reference/domain.CampaignState.qmd) | `domain/types.py` | a read-only snapshot of the store: what a player may know |

# The game loop

Every episode, scripted or LLM, is played by
[`Episode.play`](../reference/engine.episode.Episode.qmd):

```python
campaign = self.env.campaign
while not campaign.is_finished():
    if not await self.player.play_round(campaign):
        break                     # the player ended the episode early
await self.player.finish(campaign)
campaign.settle()                 # collect results still outstanding
return Played(score=self.env.score(), stopped=campaign.stopped)
```

A campaign is finished when it is stopped, or when its rounds or its budget are used
up. What a round looks like is up to the player.

**A scripted player** reads `campaign.state()`, asks its policy for a batch
(`policy.choose(state, batch_size, rng)`, with a generator seeded by the episode seed
and the round), and calls `campaign.submit(ids)`. An empty batch means "stop": the
player calls `campaign.stop(...)` and ends the episode. The policy itself only ever
sees the snapshot.

**An LLM player** makes model calls ("turns"). Each reply may call tools; every call
goes to the MCP server and comes back as a tool message. A round is over after the
turn in which the clock moved (a batch was bought, or a round was waited out) or the
campaign finished. The conversation and the turn count carry over from one round to
the next, so the whole episode is one conversation of at most 40 turns. The episode
also ends early if the model replies without calling a tool, or if the turn limit is
reached. `finish` then asks the model, without tools, for a closing summary.

The model never holds a Python object. A tool call travels like this:

```{d2}
direction: right
llm: "LLMPlayer\none turn"
bridge: "McpBridge\nJSON specs and results"
server: "MCP server\nonly the condition's tools"
toolbox: "Toolbox\none method per tool"
campaign: "Campaign"
llm -> bridge -> server -> toolbox -> campaign
```

The tools read [`CampaignState`](../reference/domain.CampaignState.qmd) snapshots, and
two of them act on the campaign: `submit_batch` calls `Campaign.submit` and `wait`
calls `Campaign.wait`. (`stop` calls `Campaign.stop`, and `propose_batch` records a
proposal without buying it.)

# The life of a batch

## The clock

Time is counted in rounds. There are two clocks, one in the store (`state.clock`) and
one in the backend, and the campaign always moves both together: `Campaign._tick`
calls `backend.advance()` and then `store.set_clock(clock + 1)`. Only two actions move
time, one round each: `Campaign.submit` and `Campaign.wait`. A real lab has no
`advance`; time simply passes, and the live backend will not need one.

A game's `delay` says how many rounds a result takes. A batch bought at clock `t`
arrives when the clock reaches `t + delay`. Most games have `delay = 0`; N-dev-delay2
has 2.

## Buying a batch: `Campaign.submit`

```{d2}
shape: sequence_diagram
player: "player or tool"
campaign: Campaign
store: CampaignStore
backend: ReplayBackend

player -> campaign: "submit(ids)"
campaign -> campaign: "_validate(state, ids)"
campaign -> store: "record_batch (PROPOSED)"
campaign -> backend: "submit(batch)"
backend -> campaign: "SubmissionHandle (replay-3)"
campaign -> store: "SUBMITTED, backend_ref; event submission_clock"
campaign -> backend: "poll(handle) for every pending batch"
backend -> campaign: "outcomes now due"
campaign -> store: "record_outcomes, COMPLETE"
campaign -> backend: "advance()"
campaign -> store: "set_clock(clock + 1)"
campaign -> backend: "poll(handle) again"
backend -> campaign: "outcomes due after the tick"
campaign -> store: "record_outcomes, COMPLETE"
campaign -> player: "SubmitResult: batch id, status, what arrived, rounds left"
```

Step by step:

1. **Check the rules.** `_validate` reads only the snapshot and raises on the first
   broken rule: stopped, no rounds left, empty, too large, duplicates, unknown design,
   already bought, over budget. Nothing has been written yet.
2. **Record the batch.** If the same designs were proposed earlier
   (`propose_batch`), that proposal is the batch; otherwise a new batch `b00n` is
   recorded as `PROPOSED`.
3. **Hand it to the lab.** `backend.submit(batch)` checks the designs exist and were
   never submitted, notes the round it was submitted in, and returns a
   `SubmissionHandle`, a receipt with a reference such as `replay-3`. If the backend
   refuses, the campaign deletes the batch it just recorded, so nothing was bought.
4. **Mark it submitted.** The store sets the batch to `SUBMITTED` with the reference;
   the campaign keeps the handle in `_handles`; an event records the clock at
   submission (what a restart needs, below).
5. **Collect, tick, collect.** The campaign polls every outstanding batch, moves both
   clocks one round, and polls again. The first collection is what lets a game with no
   delay return a batch's results in the same call. The second picks up batches that
   come due because the clock moved: in a game with a delay, the batch bought two
   rounds ago.

`submit` returns what arrived during the call. With no delay that is the batch's own
results; with a delay it may be nothing, or an earlier batch.

## Collecting results: `poll`

The receipt is what a real lab gives back too: the Foundry API returns an order id,
and results are fetched with it. In the replay, `poll(handle)` looks the reference up
(an unknown reference raises `BackendError`), and compares the backend's clock with the
round of submission:

* clock `>=` submitted at `+ delay`: `COMPLETE`, with every outcome of the batch;
* otherwise: `SUBMITTED`, with no outcomes.

Polling is cumulative (each call returns everything released so far), so polling
twice does no harm. The campaign records the outcomes not seen before, moves the
batch's status forward (`SUBMITTED → COMPLETE`, or `PARTIAL` for a lab that releases
part of a batch), and forgets the handle once the batch is complete.

## The other actions

| action | moves the clock | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Campaign.propose(ids)` | no | records a `PROPOSED` batch; buys nothing |
| `Campaign.submit(ids)` | one round | buys a batch (above) |
| `Campaign.wait()` | one round | lets a round pass without buying; allowed only while results are outstanding |
| `Campaign.ingest()` | no | polls without moving time; in a replay it always finds nothing new, since every poll already happened at the last tick |
| `Campaign.stop(reason)` | no | ends buying for good; outstanding results still arrive |
| `Campaign.settle()` | until nothing is outstanding | waits round after round; `Episode.play` calls it at the end so the score covers every purchase |

## Batch states

```text
PROPOSED ──submit──> SUBMITTED ──poll──> COMPLETE
                         └──poll──> PARTIAL ──poll──> COMPLETE   (a lab that releases part of a batch)
```

The store refuses to move a batch backwards.

## Scoring

After `settle`, `ReplayEnvironment.score()` turns the final snapshot into a
[`ScoreCard`](../reference/engine.ScoreCard.qmd): hits, purchases, the hit curve in
purchase order, distinct hit families and the best Kd. The family count uses the
sequence clusters, which only the scoring context holds; nothing gives a player the
score card or the clusters.

## Resuming after a crash

The store is written as things happen, one transaction per change. If the process
dies, `build_replay_campaign` opens the same store, rebuilds a fresh backend by
replaying every submission at its recorded clock (`restore_backend`), and checks that
each replayed submission gets the same reference as before. The campaign then rebuilds
its handles from the store, and play continues where it stopped.

# What keeps the results hidden

The question to ask is: who holds a reference to the backend, which holds every
result? The answer is the campaign (`Campaign._backend`), and so everything that holds
the campaign: the `ReplayEnvironment`, the `Episode`, the `Player`, and the tools'
`ToolContext`. Python has no private attributes, so any code running in the process
could follow those references (`campaign._backend._outcomes`), or walk the garbage
collector, or simply read `data/processed/outcomes.parquet` from disk. **Nothing in
the process enforces the leak rule against code that is determined to break it.** What
the rule rests on depends on the player.

**The LLM agent: a real boundary.** The model does not run in the process. All it can
send is tool calls, each a tool name and JSON arguments, to the tools its condition
registered on the MCP server; any other name is refused. There is no tool that runs
code, so the model has no `getattr` to reach for. Each tool is a fixed method that
builds its answer from `campaign.state()` (or the store's recorded predictions), and a
snapshot holds only delivered results. So for the agent, the guarantee is as strong as
the tool code is correct, and that is tested: `tests/test_tools_leaks.py` plays a game
through every tool and scans every response for sequences, real design ids, and outcome
fields of designs that were not bought and delivered.

**Scripted policies: a convention, checked.** A policy receives a frozen snapshot and a
seeded generator, nothing else; it cannot reach the backend through its arguments.
`tests/test_import_boundaries.py` makes sure `policies` and `advisor` never import
`engine`, `store` or `backends`. But a policy is Python in the same process, so the
rest is review: the policies are our own code, written against the snapshot.

**The players and the engine: trusted code.** `ScriptedPlayer` and `LLMPlayer` hold
the campaign itself. They use it only through its public methods: the scripted player
to read the state and buy, the LLM player to watch the clock and see whether the game
is over.

Making the in-process guarantee hard would mean a process boundary: run the player
in another process and send it serialized snapshots only, or put the lab in another
process. The live backend gets the second for free, since the outcomes will sit at
Adaptyv's API until they are released. For the replay it was not worth it: the only
player not written in this repository is the model, and it already sits behind MCP.
`replaylab serve` goes one step further and runs the tools in a separate process,
spoken to over stdio.
